conflict_topics: responsibility and entitlement (who buys supplies vs. who cleans)
dialogue_quality_notes: Agents give concrete, role-based reasons (A: buys soap/gas; D: arrives home weeknights), which makes the exchange realistic.
Conversation stays on-topic and factual; no role confusion or contradictory environment claims.
No concrete proposals (e.g., a schedule or cleaning rota) are offered — discussion remains at complaint/clarification level.
evaluation.final_reason: No substantive settlement was reached. Multiple incompatible demands remain: D wants a "fair shot" at the stove on weeknights (Agent D: "Just a fair shot at it"), A resists the implication of always giving that time (Agent A: "So you expect the stove to be free always at 7 or 8 PM?"), B insists the smell must be "sorted out" (Agent B: "But the smell still needs sorting out."), and C demands shared cleaning because of a dirty pan (Agent C: "We still have a dirty pan from last night in the sink."). No participant accepts another's proposal or offers a concrete, mutually agreed arrangement; therefore the conflict remains unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent D softened language over rounds: from general complaint to a narrower request — initial: "it is impossible to use the stove on weeknights." Later: "No, not always. Just a fair shot at it, you know?"
Agent A moved from defensive justification (buying supplies) to seeking clarification about timing: "What time is that usually?" but did not concede any obligation to change behavior.
Agents B and C maintained their positions about smell and cleaning without offering a compromise; no participant accepted another's demand.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B: "But the smell still needs sorting out." vs Agent A: "I cook most nights ... I buy most of the dish soap and gas. No one ever mentions that." — a clear substantive disagreement about responsibility for the smell and fairness of kitchen use.
Agent D: "When can I cook if it's always busy like this?" vs Agent A: "Always busy? There are other times." — introduces a new, substantive dispute about stove availability/scheduling.

Agent D clarifies: "weeknights, when I get home, it's pretty much always busy." Agent A asks for specifics: "What time is that usually?" — conflict remains but the exchange shifts toward clarification rather than escalation.

Agent C raises a separate hygiene complaint: "We still have a dirty pan from last night in the sink." Combined with the ongoing scheduling complaint (Agent D: "Usually around 7 or 8 PM."), multiple unresolved issues now coexist.

Agent A challenges D's expectation: "So you expect the stove to be free always at 7 or 8 PM?" Agent D softens: "No, not always. Just a fair shot at it, you know?" — positions clarified but incompatibilities (what is 'fair') remain.

Agent B pushes back and links issues: "A fair shot for who? And how does that stop the smell?" Agent C reiterates the cleanliness demand: "the dirty pan still here. It's about everyone doing their part." — multiple unresolved, opposing expectations (fair scheduling, smell mitigation, shared cleaning).

substantive_insights: Tension between perceived entitlement and contribution: A cites buying soap/gas as justification for cooking frequency, which other housemates do not accept as resolving smell or cleaning obligations.
Scheduling vs. hygiene are distinct but linked problems: D's request for fair stove access (7–8 PM) conflicts with A's existing cooking times and with C/B's demand about cleaning and smells.
Household lacks agreed norms or processes: complaints are raised but no mechanism (rota, ventilation practice, or explicit cleaning duty) is proposed.
